title: Joel 3:17–21
context: Joel 3:17–21 closes the book with the LORD’s promise, spoken in the first person, that his people will know him as the LORD their God, “dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain” (3:17). Versification: English 2:28–32 is Hebrew 3:1–5, and English chapter 3 is Hebrew chapter 4; this page keeps the WEB numbers. Jerusalem will be holy, and no strangers will pass through her any more; Isaiah 52:1 and Revelation 21:27 voice related hopes in their own settings. The mountains will drop sweet wine and the hills flow with milk, a picture close to Amos 9:13, and a fountain will flow out from the LORD’s house to water the valley of Shittim (3:18). Shittim means acacias. The name recalls the camp east of the Jordan in Numbers 25:1 and Joshua 2:1, but here it may describe a dry acacia valley, and some readers think of the Kidron running down toward the Dead Sea; the location is uncertain. Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8 also picture water flowing from the temple or from Jerusalem; they are named here as related images, not as one prophecy. Egypt and Edom will become desolate for the violence done to Judah and for shedding innocent blood in their land (3:19). Obadiah 10–14 accuses Edom of violence against Judah, but Joel names no occasion, and suggested background events for both nations are uncertain. Verse 21 is difficult. The verb rendered cleanse is commonly used for holding someone innocent or acquitting, and translations differ on whether the line means the LORD pardoning guilt that remains or the LORD declaring that the innocent blood of 3:19 will not go unanswered; readers in both traditions hold each view. The book ends on the words “the LORD dwells in Zion” (3:21). Historical, typological, and future readings of these promises, relating them to Judah’s return, to the church, to a future for Israel, or to the new creation, appear in both traditions, and no choice is made among them here. On vengeance for the blood of God’s people, compare the Psalms 79:6 and Psalms 58:10 boxes. Shared ground: the LORD’s presence with his people is the goal of the whole book.

verses.text: “So you will know that I am the LORD, your God, dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain. Then Jerusalem will be holy, and no strangers will pass through her any more.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says his people will know that he is the LORD their God, dwelling in Zion, his holy mountain. Arminian readers see the knowledge of God as the goal of all the judgment and restoration in the chapter, a relationship in which the people know and trust the God who saves them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “I am the LORD, your God, dwelling in Zion” as covenant language, God present among the people he has claimed. Readers in both traditions take “no strangers will pass through her” as holiness and security, relating it to Isaiah 52:1 and Revelation 21:27 in different ways.

verses.text: It will happen in that day, that the mountains will drop down sweet wine, the hills will flow with milk, all the brooks of Judah will flow with waters; and a fountain will flow out from the LORD’s house, and will water the valley of Shittim.
verses.arminianNotes: The promise pictures plenty: mountains dropping sweet wine, hills flowing with milk, and brooks full of water, close to Amos 9:13. Arminian readers see a reversal of the locusts and drought of chapters 1–2, and they read the abundance as God’s generous answer to a people who returned to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers focus on the fountain flowing from the LORD’s house to water the valley of Shittim, and they compare Ezekiel 47:1–12 and Zechariah 14:8 as related images, not one prophecy. The valley’s location is uncertain, and both traditions hold literal, typological, and new-creation readings.

verses.text: Egypt will be a desolation and Edom will be a desolate wilderness, for the violence done to the children of Judah, because they have shed innocent blood in their land.
verses.arminianNotes: Egypt will be a desolation and Edom a desolate wilderness for the violence done to Judah and the innocent blood shed in their land. Arminian readers note that the judgment is tied to specific violence, and they see God holding nations accountable for what they have done to the defenseless.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Egypt and Edom as long-standing enemies of God’s people, compare Obadiah 10–14 on Edom, and they read the verse as God’s justice for the innocent. The text names no occasion, and the historical events sometimes suggested behind it remain uncertain in both traditions.

verses.text: But Judah will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.
verses.arminianNotes: Judah will be inhabited forever and Jerusalem from generation to generation, in contrast to the desolation of Egypt and Edom. Arminian readers read the promise as God’s lasting faithfulness to his covenant people, held out to all who call on his name as in 2:32.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the promise as the certain permanence of God’s people, because it rests on his own commitment. Readers in both traditions differ on whether it looks to a restored nation, to the church, or to the new creation, and that difference does not follow Arminian and Reformed lines.

verses.text: I will cleanse their blood that I have not cleansed, for the LORD dwells in Zion.”
verses.arminianNotes: “I will cleanse their blood that I have not cleansed” is a difficult line, and translations differ. Readers in both traditions take it either as the LORD answering the innocent blood of 3:19 so that it does not go unanswered, or as the LORD cleansing guilt that remained; Arminian readers who favor pardon connect it with the call to return in 2:12–13.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verb is commonly used for acquitting or holding innocent, and those who favor pardon connect it with God’s gracious cleansing of his people, while others read it as vindication of shed blood. Shared ground: the book ends on “the LORD dwells in Zion.”
